title: Kannappa the Hunter
hookLine: a hunter brings Shiva water carried in his mouth and meat he has tasted first
carry: the heart is the real offering

cards: Water, carried up a hill in a man's mouth, because he has no pot. Wildflowers tucked into his hair, because his hands are full. A piece of roasted meat, which he has bitten into first, to make sure it's tender and good.

A young hunter climbs into a forest shrine and lays all this before Shiva. He spits the water over the stone to wash it, shakes the flowers from his hair, sets down the meat, and stands guard all night with his bow.
Today, the hunter the Tamil Shaiva saints call Kannappa.

teach.h: A PRIEST WHO GRIEVES EACH MORNING
teach.b: The Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The shrine already has a priest, a careful man who comes each morning with pure water and proper flowers.
Each morning he finds the place littered with bones and wilted blossoms, grieves, cleans it all, and worships again. At last Shiva tells him: hide tomorrow, and watch.
The hunter arrives and sees blood running from one eye of Shiva's image. Herbs don't stop it. So he takes an arrow, cuts out his own eye, and presses it to the place.
The bleeding stops, and he laughs with joy.
Then the other eye of the image begins to bleed. He sets his foot on it to mark the spot, and raises the arrow again. And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and holds his hand.
Stop, Kannappa. The story doesn't mock the priest. His worship was right.
But Shiva lets him see a love that knew none of the rules and held nothing back.
That's bhakti at its rawest: what God receives is the heart inside the offering. Krishna says it in the Gita too, in paraphrase: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, some water, offered with love, I accept.
And Sundarar, in a hymn listing the Lord's servants, names the hunter among them. One thing, plainly: this is a story about love, not a model to copy, and Shiva himself stops the hand.

teach.b: If you ever feel pulled to hurt yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

how: Kannappa is honored among the Nayanmars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country, and his story is told at the Shiva temple of Kalahasti, the hill shrine where tradition places it.

games.q: what does “tamil shaivism and the tevaram” mean?
o: a priest's rulebook for the right way to offer flowers
a hunter's chant sung to guard a shrine at night
Tamil Shiva devotion, whose saints include a hunter

games.q: the hunter's offering — tap the pairs.
p: tasted first, to be sure it was good
set on the image to mark the place

s: the story mocks the priest's careful worship
his worship is right, and Shiva honors it by letting him see a second kind of love.
Kannappa sets his foot on the image so he can find the spot
with his second eye gone, he'd need it to mark the place.
the story quietly drops the parts that break the rules
the meat, the water from his mouth and the foot all stay in.

games.q: you're the hunter. you've given one eye to stop the bleeding, and now the image's other eye bleeds. what do you do?
o: mark the spot with your foot and raise the arrow again.
pray and wait for it to stop.
games.why: he marks the spot with his foot and lifts the arrow to his second eye, and Shiva's hand comes out of the stone to stop him.

practice: If you keep a shrine or a puja shelf, offer one thing today just as it comes: a flower from outside, a glass of water, a little of your meal before you eat it, the way many Hindu families do. Don't polish it first.
If you don't pray, give someone you love what's really in your hands, a tired hour, a short call, a clumsy thank-you, and let that be enough.

wordCard.voice: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram: Kannappa, the hunter who gave his eye to stop Shiva's image bleeding, and was stopped by Shiva's own hand. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the heart is the real offering. Water from a mouth, and a hand from the stone. Rest well.
